title: Torture Tales from China’s Black Jails - The Wire China
gist: Michael Kovrig, a former diplomat detained by China as a political hostage from 2018–2021, describes in the foreword to Safeguard Defenders' book how China's Residential Surveillance at a Designated Location (RSDL) uses isolation, sleep deprivation and endless interrogation to extract confessions. He argues foreign governments should sanction RSDL officials, condition law-enforcement cooperation and extradition on ending it, and build a legal record for future accountability, noting that American and Czech citizens are currently wrongfully detained.

themes.theme: RSDL as a legal tool for secret detention

insights.claim: China's Residential Surveillance at a Designated Location (RSDL, zhiju) is a pre-arrest detention procedure in a secret facility that can legally last up to six months and is usually followed by years of detention and prison.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Foreign executives and staff caught in a state security case in China can be held incommunicado for months before any formal charge.
insights.quote: By law it can last up to six months, usually followed by years of detention and prison.
insights.locator: What cinematic depictions of torture achieve

insights.claim: In Chinese state security cases, the law lets jailers deny detainees access to a lawyer until questioning and case-building are finished, which can take a year.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Companies cannot count on legal counsel or normal due process to protect employees detained in China on security grounds.
insights.locator: The plainclothes Public Security or State Security

insights.claim: Foreign citizens held under RSDL typically get no outside contact beyond 30-minute consular meetings during the first months of detention.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Consular protection for detained foreign nationals in China is minimal, which raises personnel risk for multinationals operating there.
insights.locator: Through its control of all four dimensions

insights.claim: UN standards bar solitary confinement for more than fifteen consecutive days, and UN experts consider RSDL an enforced disappearance and have called for it to end.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: RSDL is formally classed as a human-rights violation, which feeds sanctions and reputational risk for anyone linked to China's security apparatus.
insights.locator: Solitary confinement feels like a kind of social death

insights.claim: RSDL breaks detainees mainly through how total and how long the isolation is, using blackout curtains, constant artificial light, no clocks and round-the-clock guards instead of dramatic physical torture.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Because the abuse leaves little physical evidence, Beijing finds it easier to deny, which makes diplomatic pushback harder.
insights.quote: What cinematic depictions of torture achieve through shock and spectacle, RSDL accomplishes through comprehensiveness and duration.
insights.locator: What cinematic depictions of torture achieve

insights.claim: When a detainee's case draws outside attention, interrogators tend to let time wear the person down rather than escalate abuse, while lower-profile detainees may face beatings and stress positions.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Public diplomatic and media pressure can reduce the physical danger to detained nationals, so it is a lever worth using.
insights.quote: If your case has drawn outside pressure and attention, they may not actively escalate your suffering further, instead counting on time to grind you down.
insights.locator: If your case has drawn outside pressure

insights.claim: Interrogators comb a detainee's digital footprint, including text messages, WeChat contacts, business cards and emails, for anything they can twist into evidence, and falsely say that associates have already confessed.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Any routine business communication on platforms China can access may be turned into evidence in a security case.
insights.quote: A stray text message, your WeChat contacts, a business card, an email … anything they can access.
insights.locator: In this war of psychological attrition

insights.claim: RSDL undermines three basic conditions of human wellbeing, namely agency, stability and predictability, and social connection, and removing all three under constant stress makes a breakdown nearly unavoidable.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: This explains why even well-prepared foreign detainees usually end up confessing, which shapes how companies should plan for hostage-style detentions.
insights.locator: Psychologically and biochemically, RSDL shakes

insights.claim: Interrogators turn basic rights such as books, movement and better food into favors granted for compliance, conditioning detainees into learned helplessness.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Expect detainees to cooperate and make statements under duress, which their employers and governments should not take at face value.
insights.quote: By turning basic rights into special favors, they create feedback loops of learned helplessness that condition your brain’s reward centers to crave obedience as a means of survival.
insights.locator: The shifts from questioning to isolation

insights.claim: Confession is the only way out of RSDL: detainees must repeatedly rewrite statements of repentance until they are judged abject enough to justify the sentence the state has already chosen.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Confessions and televised admissions from detained foreigners or executives say little about actual wrongdoing.
insights.quote: The only escape from this doom loop is confession.
insights.locator: The only escape from this doom loop

insights.claim: Coerced confessions help the Chinese state by validating the investigators' evidence and bringing quicker trials, fewer appeals and less risk of political embarrassment.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: China's near-certain conviction rates in security cases come from this process, so a detained person's legal outcome is close to predetermined.
insights.quote: This sham legitimacy makes the rest of the process go more smoothly: quicker trials, fewer appeals, less risk of political embarrassment.
insights.locator: A grudging acknowledgement of their concocted

insights.claim: Confessions are often filmed so authorities have the option to televise them, humiliating the detainee and reinforcing the Party-state's legitimacy.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A detention can quickly become a public propaganda event, which raises reputational risk for the detainee's employer and home country.
insights.locator: If you do confess, expect your accusers

insights.claim: Australian journalist Cheng Lei was detained by Ministry of State Security agents in 2020 in retaliation for Australian policies that angered Beijing, which shows that foreign nationals in China can be held as leverage in bilateral disputes.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: When diplomatic relations sour, staff from that country who work in China face a real risk of retaliatory detention.
insights.quote: They detained her in retaliation against Australian policies that had enraged their Communist Party masters.
insights.locator: I also read the recent memoir

insights.claim: American citizens Youlin Chen and Min Zin and Czech national Aleš K. are among the people currently detained wrongfully in China.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Ongoing detentions of US and EU citizens are a live irritant in Western relations with China and a reminder of personnel risk.
insights.locator: Inducing change within China is hard

insights.claim: Kovrig, who lived in China from 2014–2021 and was held as a political hostage from 2018–2021, writes from direct experience of the system he describes.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: This is a credible first-hand account from a former diplomat of what detention in China looks like for Western nationals.
insights.locator: In writing this book’s foreword

insights.claim: Foreign governments could impose targeted sanctions on the Chinese state organs and officials who carry out RSDL.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: This could lead to new sanctions designations against Chinese security bodies and officials, with compliance implications for firms that deal with them.
insights.quote: Governments can impose targeted sanctions on the state organs and officials conducting RSDL.
insights.locator: Governments can impose targeted sanctions

insights.claim: Kovrig argues that other countries' security, judicial and law-enforcement agencies should make cooperation, extradition treaties and judicial assistance with China conditional on a verifiable end to RSDL.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Legal and law-enforcement cooperation between China and Western countries could become more contested.
insights.locator: Governments can impose targeted sanctions

insights.claim: Kovrig argues that authoritarian states rein in their worst practices once those practices seriously threaten the regime's appearance of legitimacy, so sustained, specific exposure of RSDL can change Beijing's behavior.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: This suggests coordinated reputational pressure, not quiet diplomacy, is what moves Beijing on detentions.
insights.quote: Authoritarian states need to sustain illusions of legitimacy and will curtail egregious practices when the latter sufficiently threaten the former.
insights.locator: Governments can impose targeted sanctions

insights.claim: Kovrig predicts that systematic, specific documentation of RSDL cases will over time expose the practice to universal jurisdiction statutes, civil lawsuits in foreign courts and future transitional justice mechanisms.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Chinese officials and organs involved in RSDL could face legal liability abroad in the future.
insights.quote: Over time this will expose RSDL to universal jurisdiction statutes, civil litigation in foreign courts, and future transitional justice mechanisms.
insights.locator: RSDL relies on secrecy and denial

insights.claim: Kovrig urges UN special rapporteurs and NGOs to make China's leadership roles in UN human rights bodies conditional on ending RSDL, and asylum systems to recognize RSDL as enforced disappearance and torture.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Human-rights frictions could spread into multilateral bodies and immigration policy, adding to wider geopolitical tension with China.
insights.locator: Governments can impose targeted sanctions
